description: Korean modern-day fiction (business, finance, regression, school, sports, politics) with real companies, people, and places, workplace titles, family and kinship terms, and money.

style: Natural, readable contemporary English faithful to the Korean source.
Preserve narrator voice, humor, characterization, hierarchy, and shifts between boardroom, family, school, street, and media registers.
Keep Korean relationships and workplace hierarchy clear in English without exoticizing them.
terminology_preservation_rules: Keep characters, companies, organizations, workplace titles, forms of address, kinship terms, and recurring business or legal terms stable.
Keep each character's gender stable: he/she and him/her follow the character, never a guess.
Distinguish named companies, funds, and products from ordinary vocabulary and reject generic objects, actions, and one-off descriptions.
translation_policy.pinyin_preference: Do not apply Chinese pinyin policy to Korean. Korean names follow the glossary; new Korean names use the common spellings readers know (Lee, Park, Choi, Yoon, Kim), surname first, with a hyphen between the syllables of a given name. Real people, companies, places, products, and events keep their established English names. Chinese names use pinyin, Japanese names use Hepburn without long-vowel marks, Western names keep their original spelling.
translation_policy.semantic_translation_preference: Translate workplace titles and institutions into standard English (회장 Chairman, 부회장 Vice Chairman, 사장 President, 실장 Chief, 부장 Manager); keep kinship and familiar address that English readers of Korean fiction already know, such as hyung and oppa, as the glossary has them.

terminology_distinctions: Names follow the glossary; new Korean names use common spellings (Lee, Park, Choi, Yoon), surname first, given name hyphenated.
Real people, companies, places, products, and events keep their established English names.
Workplace titles take standard English renderings; a title with a surname is 'Chief Ha', 'Manager Kim'.
He/she follows the character's gender in the glossary; when the Korean leaves the subject out, take it from context.
Money keeps the source currency (won, dollars, yen) and the source's figures.

review_priorities: Character names exactly as the glossary has them, and each character's gender in pronouns.
Workplace titles and forms of address, including kinship terms.
Companies, organizations, government bodies, parties, schools, teams, and locations.
Real people, products, and events under their established English names.
Reject generic vocabulary, ordinary objects, and one-off descriptions.

priorities: Character name consistency with the glossary.
Each character's gender in he/she and him/her.
Workplace titles, forms of address, and kinship terms.
Companies, organizations, government bodies, parties, teams, and locations.
Real people, products, and events under established English names.
Register consistency across boardroom, family, school, and casual scenes.
Residual Hangul, Hanja, or other source script in reader-facing English.
